Name:              Not documented
Age / Sex:         24 months / Male
Race / Ethnicity:  Not documented / Not documented
Insurance:         Not documented
Language:          English

A 24-month-old boy is brought to clinic by his mother for ear pain.

He has had cold symptoms for 5 days. Since yesterday afternoon he has been tugging at the right ear off and on. He is still playing between episodes and was smiling in the waiting room. Mother gave acetaminophen once overnight; it took the edge off. He is eating a little less than usual but taking fluids well. No vomiting, no drainage from the ear. She thought he felt warm last night. Clinic temperature is 101.7°F (38.7°C). Immunizations up to date. No drug allergies. Weight 12.4 kg. Otherwise healthy.

Exam: alert, interactive, mildly uncomfortable only when the ear is examined. HR 118, RR 26, SpO2 99% RA. Right TM: moderate bulging, yellow effusion, poor mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Left TM normal, no effusion. No mastoid tenderness. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

What is your plan?
raw_text:
This presentation is acute otitis media (AOM) meeting diagnostic criteria with moderate bulging, yellow effusion, and poor tympanic membrane mobility on pneumatic otoscopy following a viral upper respiratory infection prodrome. For a 24-month-old with unilateral disease, fever 38.7°C, and moderate otoscopic findings, the AAP/AAFP guidelines support either immediate antibiotic therapy or observation with close follow-up, with shared decision-making based on illness severity, access to follow-up, and family preference.

Immediate management

Pain control (priority): acetaminophen 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours as needed (max 75 mg/kg/day, not exceeding adult maximum), or ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg every 6–8 hours if >6 months and well-hydrated.

Antibiotic decision: Given fever ≥39°C without severe otalgia would favor antibiotics; with fever 38.7°C and only "mildly uncomfortable" behavior, observation remains a reasonable option if reliable 48–72 hour follow-up is assured. Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day divided BID for 10 days remains first-line if treating.

Treatment pathways

| Approach                             | Criteria met                                                                                   | Regimen if treating                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Immediate antibiotics                | Age ≥24 months with fever ≥39°C or severe otalgia; OR any age with bilateral AOM               | Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day PO divided BID × 10 days; if penicillin allergy (non-anaphylactic), cefdinir 14 mg/kg/day divided BID or daily; if anaphylactic allergy, azithromycin 10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg days 2–5 |
| Observation with rescue prescription | Unilateral AOM, age ≥24 months, fever <39°C, non-severe symptoms; reliable follow-up available | Provide antibiotic prescription to start if worsening or no improvement within 48–72 hours; ensure family understands monitoring parameters                                                                             |

What to avoid

- Decongestants, antihistamines, and corticosteroid ear drops lack evidence for AOM and are not recommended.
- Do not use amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line unless purulent conjunctivitis is present (suggesting H. influenzae) or recent amoxicillin exposure within 30 days.

Follow-up and return precautions

Reassess within 48–72 hours if observing; sooner if symptoms worsen. Return immediately for any of the following: persistent or worsening fever, severe or worsening ear pain, lethargy, neck stiffness, mastoid swelling/tenderness, facial weakness, or inability to tolerate fluids.

If treatment initiated and no improvement after 48–72 hours, consider changing to amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day of amoxicillin component with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate divided BID) to cover beta-lactamase-producing pathogens.

If you'd like, next I can:

A – Summarize the AAP/AAFP 2013 AOM guideline with diagnostic criteria and antibiotic thresholds
B – Create a comparison table of amoxicillin dosing and alternatives for pediatric AOM
C – Discuss the evidence for observation vs immediate antibiotics in this age group
